title: Cellular competencies come by default, unlike organism-level learning

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Cellular competencies come by default, unlike organism-level learning

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Unlike organism-level learning, which requires mechanisms such as nervous systems that must themselves be evolved and paid for, cellular competencies come by default because cells already carry capabilities evolved when their ancestors were independent organisms.

fields.label: Work
fields.value: Cellular Competency during Development Alters Evolutionary Dynamics in an Artificial Embryogeny Model

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Shreesha L 2023, Cellular Competency during Development Alters Evolutionary Dynamics in an Artificial Embryogeny Model › 1. Introduction

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: In contrast, cellular competencies come “by default” because organisms consist of cellular components that already have many capabilities evolved during their ancestral lifetime as independent organisms.

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Shreesha L, Levin M, “Cellular Competency during Development Alters Evolutionary Dynamics in an Artificial Embryogeny Model”, Entropy (Basel, Switzerland) (2023), doi:10.3390/e25010131; section “1. Introduction”. Scope: Cells of multicellular organisms and their unicellular ancestors

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on levin-2023-competency-03: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.38

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Comparative molecular data can test parts of the ancestry claim. They cannot cleanly establish the broad cost contrast or that competency is automatically available to multicellular evolution.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Compare phylogenetically reconstructed cellular sensing and action machinery with organism-level learning machinery, measuring whether multicellular lineages inherit rather than newly evolve each capacity and its energetic cost. Support requires ancestral cellular competencies to precede and reduce the evolutionary cost of developmental control.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
'By default' and 'paid for' lack unique quantitative definitions.

Deep ancestral capabilities are reconstructed indirectly.

Cellular and organismal mechanisms overlap.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
operationalizability: 0.48
data adequacy: 0.28
analysis feasibility: 0.35
data existence: 0.42
discriminating power: 0.34

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The contrast is empirical in principle: costs and phylogenetic origins could be measured. Comparative descriptions of unicellular behaviour exist, but they do not contain the cost accounting the claim requires, and the authors note elsewhere that real competency costs are unmeasured. Existing observations do not yet decide it.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Compare the fitness cost of building a learning nervous system with the marginal cost of cellular sensing, sorting and motility in multicellular species, against the presence of those cellular behaviours in unicellular relatives. Competencies that are phylogenetically ancestral and costless to maintain would support the claim; a measurable extra cost, or independent origin inside metazoans, would count against 'by default'.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Presence of similar behaviours in unicells does not show they were retained for free.

No public dataset prices the marginal cost of cellular competencies against the cost of nervous-system learning.
